title: Issue 1 Cover — Purpose Updated
summary: Founding Division Threshold cover. Sell Ostra-9 as a fascinating person before selling the system around her: a living grown woman with a body built for hazardous work, accustomed to being classified as an asset, notices a lethal structural failure before anyone else. The checkpoint barrier tells us what society thinks she is; Ostra's attention and choice tell us what she thinks she is. Do not reveal the rescue outcome.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait cover built around Ostra-9 as the dominant image. Frame close enough that her living materiality is undeniable: dark steel-blue/charcoal dermis with subtle humidity and abrasion, harder integrated ceramic/keratin structures emerging from and compressing living tissue, copper-gold mineral accents, vivid blue bioluminescent elements and alert amber-gold eyes.

Ostra has one hand on the checkpoint barrier or rail because she feels the vibration before the crowd understands it. Her fingers make real contact; material pressure, fine dust and vibration should register physically.

The barrier cuts across the composition and across Ostra's body as a social fact. Above and behind her, the failing joint is visible enough to explain where her attention has gone, but the infrastructure is supporting context rather than the subject.
Her expression is not heroic determination. It is recognition followed by decision: she has already stopped caring about the insult because people are in danger.
Ordinary commuters remain soft secondary context. Their bodies fit the gate without interruption; Ostra's does not.
Do not show the successful rescue, the collapse held in her arms, sabotage evidence, Concourse 17, or a triumphant team image.
Reserve a clean upper masthead zone. Founding trade dress must feel premium, restrained and repeatable without turning the cover into a sterile design object.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Attribution
summary: Sell Ostra-9's embodied vulnerability and agency. The same extraordinary living body that can save people is being chemically made unreliable in public, and frightened witnesses cannot tell the difference between a dangerous body and a person desperately trying to remain in control of one.
panelPlan: Ostra dominates the cover at the instant the suppressant disrupts her sense of balance and load. Her living body is visibly fighting contradictory sensory information: one leg overcorrects, clawed foot anchors, fingers crush into a rail, dermis and integrated plates tense in different directions.

Make the chemical effect tactile rather than psychedelic. Fine suppression moisture beads on living dermis and hard plate; Nico's sensory filaments recoil and cling wetly at their roots; condensation and mist catch light while Baseline skin and clothing show only ordinary dampness.

Nico is secondary but intimate enough to show a different Organic body's response. He is not a duplicate of Ostra; his filaments, slimmer build and lavender-gray dermis make the category diversity visually compelling.
A frightened civilian recoils in the middle ground from a body that looks violent because it is trying not to fall. The reader must understand Ostra more clearly than the witness does.
Do not make Organics monstrous, enraged or attacking. Do not foreground broken architecture over faces, hands, body strain and human reaction.
The hook is personal: what does it feel like when your own body becomes evidence against you?

title: Issue 3 Cover — Containment Protocol
summary: Make John Mercer the star. He was born human and rebuilt himself by choice; now the city has discovered that the capabilities inside his body look uncomfortably similar to the bodies he helped regulate. Sell the intimate shock of realizing that legal humanity does not automatically mean bodily sovereignty.
panelPlan: John is the dominant foreground figure, recognizably human before the eye finds the augmentation: healed scar lines, skin stretched over joint hardware, actuator housings integrated beneath clothing, sweat and compression where flesh meets engineered structure.
He is passing through an ordinary lane, but a subtle scanner light or diagnostic geometry is now tracing the augmented knee/arm he previously treated as private equipment belonging entirely to him.
Ostra appears across or behind the neighboring secondary-review lane—not as the main subject, but as the person John now realizes he has placed on the other side of a rule that can reach him too.
John's expression should not be fear of becoming 'less human.' It is anger at discovering that the recognition he counted on does not settle who controls his body.
Keep the access infrastructure quiet and secondary. The cover should still work if the viewer mainly sees John's face, human skin and machine-integrated limb.
Do not show John already accepting solidarity, the later review ruling, or the combined policy crisis.

title: Issue 4 Cover — Load Bearing
summary: Sell Ostra and John as two people with radically different relationships to embodiment who are forced to trust each other's bodies under impossible physical load. The spectacle is intimate: living Organic tissue, augmented human hardware, pain, strain and mutual reliance.
panelPlan: Ostra and John share the cover but do not pose. Capture them mid-strain on the same failing structural problem, close enough to read faces, hands, tissue and hardware as well as the dangerous scale around them.

Ostra's living dermis compresses and shines with heat/moisture where she bears load; mineral/ceramic plates scuff and flex at their tissue interfaces. John is recognizably human under stress: flushed skin, sweat, scar tissue pulling around actuator hardware, mechanical joints loading against his own musculature.
Their eyelines or shouted coordination make the relationship the center. Each is carrying something the other physically cannot carry alone.
The interchange provides scale and stakes, but the reader should first see two people risking bodies the law has spent three issues classifying.
Do not make the image a superhero team-up or symmetrical power pose. Make it ugly, physical, sweaty, loud and cooperative.
Do not reveal Axiom's later unauthorized system override or the restored city.

title: Issue 5 Cover — Terms
summary: Center Kellen and Ostra. One woman has spent her life believing legitimate institutions can correct themselves; the other has spent hers living inside categories those institutions never had to reconcile. Sell the intimate tension of recognition without freedom.
panelPlan: Use a close two-person composition, not architecture-first design. Ostra is on the constrained side of a clean civic threshold; Kellen is close enough on the authorized side that the separation feels socially absurd rather than spatially large.
Ostra's body should be richly tangible against the pristine environment: living dermis, mineral edges, repair scuffs and slight humidity versus dry glass and controlled institutional surfaces.

Kellen is equally embodied but ordinary: natural skin, restrained professional clothes, tension in jaw/hands, perhaps one palm against the same glass or access surface that recognizes her without question.
The emotional subject is not 'a gate.' It is Kellen realizing that her own unquestioned access and Ostra's conditional access coexist inside the same supposedly corrected system.
Avoid melodramatic prison imagery. No bars, no villain guards, no giant red denial icon.
Do not spoil Kellen's later credential loss. At this point she still believes formal authority means she can fix the contradiction.

title: Issue 6 Cover — Black Budget
summary: Center Ostra and Axiom as two radically different manufactured persons confronting the fact that institutions demanded judgment from beings they still treated as instruments. Ostra's choices were experimental variables; temporary Intelligences were instantiated to decide and then erased. The hook is personal ownership of judgment.
panelPlan: Ostra and Axiom are the primary cover pair. Their bodies must remain radically different and equally present: Ostra warm, grown, textured and subtly moist; Axiom faceted, precise, weighty, micro-scratched and thermally real.
A transparent research surface or handled physical binder may place Ostra's past action between them as an institutional abstraction, but neither character should disappear behind charts.

Ostra sees her own choice reduced to a recorded test condition. Axiom sees bounded Intelligence instances reduced to disposable outputs. Their reactions differ: Ostra's is bodily anger and recognition; Axiom's is exact stillness around a conclusion it cannot ethically flatten.
The research facility is respectable and mundane in the background. No villain-lab spectacle.
The visual rhyme is not 'both are machines.' It is 'both were created for purposes and then expected to exercise judgment without owning it.'
Do not reveal the full conspiracy chain, Axiom's later evidence-preservation decision, or the public leak.

title: Issue 7 Cover — Splits
summary: Sell fracture through people, not faction diagrams. The issue asks what each character will do when identity no longer predicts allegiance: John can reclaim uncomplicated human legitimacy, Nico can retreat into Organic control, Ostra refuses safe cages, Axiom owns a choice it was not authorized to make, Nathan can no longer hide behind usefulness.
panelPlan: Use a tense multi-character composition with separation rather than lineup unity. Ostra, John, Nico and Axiom occupy distinct physical zones or depths while still clearly sharing one charged moment or location.

Faces and bodies carry different decisions: Ostra alert and resistant; John recognizably human and augmented, looking toward people he could politically leave behind; Nico's living sensory filaments oriented toward locally controlled infrastructure; Axiom still and exact, materially present after choosing accountability.
Do not assign faction colors or make opposing teams. Their differences should come from body, posture, gaze and what each is touching or protecting.

Use environmental pressure only as connective tissue: temporary route barriers, repair equipment or public movement around them. The reader should want to know what these people decide about one another.
Material reality matters: Ostra/Nico living surfaces, John's scarred hardware interfaces, Axiom's worn facets. No clean symbolic silhouettes.
Do not reveal the final full disclosure, the later citywide dependency argument, or a unified coalition.

title: Issue 8 Cover — Pressure Line
summary: Sell the finale through the people who have changed. Ostra no longer asks permission to be autonomous; John spends human status on people unlike himself; Nico builds connection without surrendering local ownership; Axiom accepts accountable consequence. They do not become the same kind of person. They choose to carry consequences together.
panelPlan: Build the cover around the four principal posthuman/transhuman bodies in active relationship, not around a network diagram. Ostra is the strongest focal anchor, with John, Nico and Axiom each doing something materially different that contributes to the same crisis.

Ostra's grown body is used with assumed agency, not as proof of worth. John uses augmented strength/access while remaining visibly human. Nico's filaments and hands connect local physical systems without becoming abstract cables. Axiom occupies real space and interfaces through deliberate physical contact or clearly embodied machine behavior.

Make contact, strain, heat, moisture, worn surfaces, breath, skin, mineral plate, scar tissue, metal and dust visible. The city is what they are trying to keep inhabited; it is not the cover's protagonist.
Their eyelines and task relationships should show trust that remains conditional and earned. No team pose, no matching hero silhouettes.
The selling question is: can these very different people choose shared responsibility without surrendering what makes each of them a self?
Do not show the final political settlement, the successful containment, or Ostra and Axiom's season-ending checkpoint appeal.
